F: The action strengthens sustainable, survivor‑centred GBV prevention and response by combining public funding advocacy, flexible response financing, and improved CSO financial capacity. It advocates for the inclusion of GBV budgets and action plans in annual local government budgets, with clear targets and quarterly reviews to ensure consistent, context‑responsive funding that meets the needs of vulnerable groups. In parallel, the action establishes a collaboratively managed GBV response fund to enable rapid, unplanned support for survivors, such as safe spaces, health, legal, and protection services. Drawing on Plan and Kapal Perempuan’s proven grant management experience, the fund will be replenished through government, CSR, and community contributions, with transparent reporting. To ensure long‑term sustainability, local CSOs will receive capacity building in financial planning, grant management, and revenue diversification, supported through consortium models that provide shared compliance and governance services. This strengthens CSOs’ credibility and ability to partner with donors, particularly youth‑ and girl‑led organizations.
I: The action strengthens institutional sustainability by formally embedding local CSOs within government GBV prevention and response systems. Through Memoranda of Understanding with local authorities, CSOs’ roles in prevention, case management, and capacity building are clearly defined, reviewed annually, and supported by designated government liaison officers, ensuring long‑term ownership and integration into local agendas. Local CSOs are connected to national and thematic GBV networks and centers of excellence to promote knowledge exchange, joint initiatives, shared resources, and data‑driven monitoring. In addition, GBV prevention and response modules are institutionalized within in‑service training curricula for government staff, law enforcement, and community leaders, with regular refresher courses. This ensures sustained competencies, continuity despite staff turnover, and the normalization of GBV response as part of standard institutional practice.
E: To promote green practices in GBV governance, particularly in raising awareness and disseminating regulations, while also addressing funding limitations for delivering information and guidelines to the community and vulnerable groups and public awareness to reduce reliance on physical materials, the initiative will facilitate local CSOs to develop online dashboards and websites. The Action will also develop online modules and other tools to facilitate communication and collaborate with relevant local government units to ensure ownership of these digital systems beyond the project period. By reducing the action’s carbon footprint, digital engagement will be continuously evaluated for effectiveness, with adjustments made based on regular user feedback and technological advancements. GBV escalates in areas prone to climate and disaster risk, especially during emergencies when violence against women, children, and minority groups surges. The action will thus invite climate and humanitarian stakeholders into our GBV policy dialogue. They will share how environmental shocks and crises heighten risks for vulnerable women and girls, and propose collaborative interventions (for example, Plan is leading in Protection, Gender, and Inclusion in Anticipatory Action with pilot in flood-prone areas). Working in cross-sector dialogue will build connections and intention for cooperation. Those relationships will continue beyond project period with the leadership encourage (co-owned by) GBV and environment/humanitarian actors—that meets regularly beyond the project’s end. This group will continue exchanging updates and learning to ensure the climate–GBV dialogue remains alive.
S: The Action promotes collaboration between different actors who have a role to play in GBV response and prevention. Regular dialogue between rights holders and duty bearers in both formal and informal settings will reach less-heard voices. Sharing and linking between civil society, public and private sector actors will become normalized, strengthening the social bonds needed to prevent and respond to GBV. By supporting girls and young women to lead on inclusive campaigns the Action empowers them to claim their rights, increasing their resilience and community engagement. By engaging duty bearers in the implementation, and monitoring of gendertransformative policies addressing GBV, the Action contributes to enhancing their awareness and duty towards their constituents. By adopting a gender-transformative approach, this Action also aims to contribute to long-term social change that increases girls’/women’s agency and engages men and boys as agents of change.

Gender-based violence (GBV) remains a serious and pervasive issue in Indonesia. GBV is perpetuated by harmful stereotypes, victim-blaming, and entrenched socio-cultural attitudes. Data from KPPPA’s SIMFONI system shows that women and girls, particularly those in vulnerable groups, face significant risks of violence—including physical, psychological, and sexual abuse, as well as exploitation, trafficking, neglect, child marriage, and online GBV. Girls aged 13 to 17 experience the highest rates of violence.
Child marriage alone has profound social and economic consequences: it increases school dropout rates, raises maternal and infant mortality, and contributes to child stunting. Online GBV has surged in recent years, making up 66% of reported cases in 2023, while exposure to pornography and low digital literacy further reinforce toxic masculinity and the objectification of women. GBV is prevalent in educational settings, including religious schools. Although there are legal frameworks in place, the recurrence of GBV cases is driven by persistent socio-cultural tolerance, weak law enforcement, economic disparities, and systemic corruption. Post-disaster displacement and inadequate humanitarian responses heighten the risk of GBV in affected areas.

SUMMARY Gender-based violence (GBV) remains a serious and pervasive issue in Indonesia. Women and girls, particularly those in vulnerable groups, face significant risks of violence—including physical, psychological, and sexual abuse, as well as exploitation, trafficking, neglect, child marriage, and online GBV.
To tackle this issue, Plan International works together with KAPAL Perempuan to end GBV and build safer, more inclusive communities. The project specifically empowers civil society organisations (CSOs), as key actors in the advancement of gender equality, to address specific issues in GBV prevention and response. We further strengthen multi-sector collaboration and advocacy efforts to enhance development, implementation and monitoring of gender-transformative policies addressing GBV. And inclusive campaigns for GBV awareness are conducted, as well as community engagement led by girls and women, jointly conducted by CSOs and youth groups. The project started in November 2025.

The action applies a gender-transformative approach to strengthen the capacity and enabling environment for CSOs in advancing women’s and girls’ agency and building effective, inclusive, and community-rooted prevention and response mechanisms against GBV. This transformation is achieved through three mutually reinforcing outputs: Output 1 (CSO capacity building/rights holders– accommodative to responsive stage): 50 CSOs are strengthened in capacity and organizational sustainability. This output assumes that civil society actors have a basic organizational foundation, that civic space remains open, and that community members recognize CSOs as legitimate actors. Gender Power Mapping and Analysis enables CSOs to identify local power structures and plan redistributive and norm‑shifting strategies, resulting in inclusive, survivor‑centred GBV services for underserved groups. Output 2 (policy environment/duty bearers – redistributive stage): Strengthened CSOs will then engage wider stakeholders through multi-actor collaboration and advocacy at subnational level for GBV policy development, implementation, and monitoring. Evidence and local voices are elevated through CSO networks and media engagement, shifting decision‑making power toward women and girls. This output relies on the assumption that local and national authorities are open to civil society collaboration, and that existing coordination mechanisms can be strengthened rather than resisted. Output 3 (campaigns/community engagement – transformative stage): Community‑led campaigns, led by women and youth and engaging men, religious and customary leaders, challenge GBV myths and stigma and promote inclusive gender norms. This output assumes that media space is accessible and open, that campaign messages are context-sensitive, and that communities— including men and religious and customary groups—are willing to engage. Together, these outputs enable CSOs to act as credible change agents.

The fight against GBV in Indonesia has been a decades-long effort, driven by CSOs, women’s rights organizations, and activists. This culminated in the Sexual Violence Crime Law (UU TPKS) of April. With the law now passed, attention turns to implementation and continued efforts are necessary to fully combat GBV. Yet implementation lags: several UU TPKS regulations remain pending, no roadmap for elimination of sexual violence exists, and many law‑enforcement officers still rely on outdated Criminal Code provisions. The proposed Action builds on the collective experience and proven successes of Plan and KAPAL. Plan and KAPAL have experience in advocating for the Law on Sexual Violence Crimes (UU TPKS) and were actively involved in the judicial review of the Marriage Law, particularly in efforts to raise the minimum age of marriage for girls. In West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), Plan played a key role in the development of a Regional Regulation (Perda) on the Prevention of Child Marriage and is actively involved as part of the Task Force on the Protection of Women and Children (PPA). Plan Indonesia’s peer educator model has enabled youth to lead advocacy and policy engagement, including the Sahabat Pengadilan initiative in NTB, where young people support children resisting early marriage. At the community level, Plan supports CBCPMs, child forums, and schools to prevent child marriage and GBV. During the past 10 years, Plan has provided capacity building for more than 24 CSOs and 25 CBOs across 6 provinces. KAPAL Perempuan complements this approach through its grassroots and policy-level work. It has led campaigns to raise the legal marriage age and pioneered Gender Watch, a community-based GBV monitoring tool. Its Complaint Posts and online counseling services offer vital support for GBV survivors. Through its PPHAM program, KAPAL nurtures women human rights defenders (WHRDs) now leading GBV prevention and survivor support in Sulawesi, NTB, and North Sulawesi.KAPAL’s Sekolah Perempuan has empowered Indigenous and marginalized women to influence decisionmaking, including contributing to Munas Perempuan, which helped shape the RPJPN 2025–2045 with policy proposals from all 34 provinces.
